candidate.answerReason: The visible labels are 11, 14, and 15 on mutually adjacent faces. Of the two possible sets of six consecutive whole numbers containing these labels, only 11 through 16 permits equal sums on opposite faces.

methods.label: Test the two possible sets
methods.explanation:
The figure shows \(11\), \(14\), and \(15\) on three mutually adjacent faces. Since there are six consecutive numbers and both \(11\) and \(15\) occur, the numbers must be either \(10,11,12,13,14,15\) or \(11,12,13,14,15,16\). These are the only possibilities: starting below \(10\) would leave out \(15\), and starting above \(11\) would leave out \(11\).

For the first set, the total is \(75\). The three opposite pairs have equal sums, so each pair must sum to \(75\div3=25\). The face opposite \(11\) would therefore have to be \(25-11=14\). But those two faces are adjacent in the figure, so this set is impossible.

The remaining set works: the opposite pairs can be \((11,16)\), \((14,13)\), and \((15,12)\), each summing to \(27\). Place each unseen number opposite its indicated visible partner. Thus the total is
\[
3\times27=\boxed{81},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
